assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based framework and the trade-shock evidence changed how economists and policymakers understand technology, globalisation, local labour markets and wage inequality. The work combines new data, credible identification and a conceptual framework. It also speaks to the technological change and adjustment costs that recent prizes have highlighted.
assessment.attribution: Autor and Katz (with collaborators outside the list) are central to the task and skill-demand framework. Autor, Dorn and Hanson are central to the China-shock evidence. Autor links the two strands, with Hanson and Katz anchoring each. Dorn is a close fourth contributor, and the three-name cap forces a hard choice.
assessment.maturity: The skill-biased change literature goes back to the 1990s, and the task approach and China-shock papers date from the 2000s and 2010s. Replications, critiques and refinements have been extensive, so the core findings are well tested.
uncertainties: Dorn's exclusion is a close call.
Some China-shock magnitudes and the task-content interpretation remain debated.
Katz's contributions overlap with another ballot entry.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The heterogeneous-firm model of trade shifted the field's unit of analysis from the industry to the firm. It explains selection, exporter premia and gains from trade beyond comparative advantage. It underpins much empirical and quantitative trade work and has had wide influence on policy analysis.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the clear originator of the framework. Helpman contributed the broader monopolistic competition and firm-level theory and the empirical extensions with Melitz and Yeaple. Redding is an important extender but the credit is less concentrated in him.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of theory, structural estimation and empirical confirmation, so the contribution is firmly established.
uncertainties: Competing claims from Bernard, Jensen and others on the empirical facts about exporting firms.
Helpman also appears on another ballot entry, which may split support.
Whether the committee sees this as a theory prize or part of a wider trade prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Structural demand estimation with differentiated products (BLP) and dynamic industry models turned industrial organisation into a quantitative, policy-relevant field. It is used in merger review, antitrust and regulatory analysis, and the methods spread to trade, health and public economics.
assessment.attribution: Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes (BLP 1995) form the core of the demand-estimation contribution. Pakes also led the dynamic-games work (Ericson-Pakes, Pakes-McGuire). Bresnahan, Benkard and others are significant, but the credit most clearly sits with the BLP trio.
assessment.maturity: Three decades of use and refinement make the work mature and widely adopted.
uncertainties: The group is large, so the cutoff is somewhat arbitrary and Bresnahan's claim is substantial.
Concerns about identification assumptions and computational fragility in structural IO.
No prior IO-econometrics prize of this type, so relative standing against other fields is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Building a multi-century dataset of financial crises, defaults and debt episodes, and drawing out regularities from it, is archival economic history with a clear macroeconomic payoff. It shaped the understanding of crises, sovereign debt and policy after 2008. Its worth comes from the data and the stylised facts as well as the specific claims.
assessment.attribution: The two are credited jointly and consistently for the dataset and the main books and papers. Individual contributions are hard to separate, but joint recognition is natural.
assessment.maturity: The central work dates from about 2008–2010 and has had over fifteen years of use and extension. The data have been adopted widely.
uncertainties: The 2010 growth-and-debt threshold paper had coding and methodological errors, which may weigh on the committee's view.
Mostly descriptive rather than causal evidence.
Rogoff also appears on another ballot entry.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The misallocation framework gave a measurable account of why countries differ in aggregate productivity. It links micro-level distortions to cross-country income gaps and has guided a large literature on development, growth and policy reform, which gives it strong relevance.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow (2009) supplied the widely used measurement framework. Restuccia and Rogerson (2008) showed the aggregate impact of distortions, but Rogerson is not on the credited list. Without him the credit is incomplete, and I include Restuccia as a close substitute.
assessment.maturity: More than fifteen years of replications and extensions. The measurement approach has been refined and criticised.
uncertainties: Sensitivity to measurement error and to the treatment of adjustment costs and markups.
Restuccia–Rogerson overlap leaves attribution partly outside the ballot.
Debate over how much of the productivity gap is truly due to misallocation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Kiyotaki–Moore (1997) and the financial accelerator work show how collateral constraints amplify and propagate shocks. These are now standard in macro-finance and in the analysis of crises and policy.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki and Moore are the clear originators of the credit-cycle model. Gertler contributed to the financial accelerator and later macro-finance work (with Bernanke, who was already honoured in 2022, and with Kiyotaki). Gilchrist is an important empirical contributor but less central.
assessment.maturity: Nearly thirty years old and thoroughly embedded in teaching and policy modelling, especially after 2008.
uncertainties: Bernanke's prior prize and the credit division with Gertler are awkward.
Gertler also appears on another ballot entry.
Empirical identification of the mechanism is partly model-dependent.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Reconstructing long-run top income and wealth series from tax records is a major data-building achievement that reopened the study of inequality. Methodologically it is close to historical national accounts and archival work, and it influenced policy debate and the research agenda across many countries.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez are central to the top-incomes series and Zucman to offshore wealth and distributional accounts. Atkinson, who is deceased, was also a pioneer and cannot be credited.
assessment.maturity: The top-income work dates from the early 2000s and has been extended to many countries. The wealth and offshore work is more recent.
uncertainties: Methodological disputes over the tax-data treatment of capital income and wealth estimates.
The theoretical claims in Capital in the 21st Century were criticised.
Some work is relatively recent, and Saez also appears on another ballot entry.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data gave a new, precise measurement of intergenerational mobility and of place effects. The findings inform policy on opportunity and neighbourhoods. The measurement contribution is large and the research design is innovative.
assessment.attribution: Chetty leads the program, with Hendren and Friedman as the closest collaborators on mobility and neighbourhood effects. Katz is credited on the neighbourhood experiment work, but it is hard to rank him alongside the three. Chetty's attribution overlaps with other agendas.
assessment.maturity: About a dozen years of results. Some findings have been replicated and others are still being tested, so it is less mature than the entries ranked above.
uncertainties: Causal interpretation of place effects and sensitivity to measurement choices.
The committee may see the work as still unfolding.
Many collaborators, and Chetty's work also appears on another ballot entry.
